story_text.value:
FlightTrack was my iPhone flight tracker from the early App Store days (bestselling travel app for 4 years), and I just rewrote it from scratch.

I first wrote FlightTrack as a side project in 2008. It did really well and I quit my day job and started a company around it that was bought by Expedia in 2010; Expedia retired the app in 2017. By then I had burned out and focused my energy on classical singing, which turns out to mean living in airports. But I missed the app.

This summer I started rebuilding it from scratch, with a design inspired by Paul Mijksenaar's fantastic signage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, and working with Claude to write a server in Go and an iOS app in Swift. In 2008 v1.0 took me 6 weeks of evenings/weekends; now it took about the same amount of time, but thanks to Claude, I ended up with much more functionality (e.g. inbound flight tracking) and was able to try entire design iterations as functional code rather than just mockups.

The data is way more expensive now, so it’s a $59.99/yr subscription, but I’m giving a free year to the first 100 subscribers. I'll be adding lots of features soon but wanted to get this version out for Thanksgiving travel. Let me know anything you want and I'll do my best!

title.value: Show HN: I wrote FlightTrack twice

story_text.value:
With AI stripmining every code publicly accessible, CVE rates soaring, and maintainers under pressure, are they on their way to a burnout?

I've seen some commenters going like "just the usual stream of CVEs & fixes, business as usual". We know that's not true.

The past few weeks were exciting. PHP, eMudhra, widespread attacks on supermarket fridges, full-day+ outage of MSFT cloud systems & more. If this were a blip, okay. But some experts estimate this could be the new 'normal' for a year, 2 years or longer (until most bugs have been shaken out). Which made me think of the human aspect.

Are you maintainer of a software project affected by this? Making extra hours? Losing sleep? Is a burnout in the stars? Would that be something you could feel coming? Any way to mitigate this?

Asking because, well... if this keeps going, maintainers burn out, patching/mitigation work suffer, and obviously that would affect the public at large not just professionals.

Maybe AI can help here as well. But regardless: maintainers' lives matter (MLM).

title.value: Ask HN: CVE craziness – are you on a path to burnout?

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Jakob, the solo dev and founder behind Taskless.

I got tired of my AGENTS.md files being ignored or forgotten a half dozen turns into conversations. I also remembered reading someone here on HN saying we weren't using nearly enough syntax trees in our code checks. This is the result.

Taskless gives you powerful syntax tree tools with human verifiable fixtures. The CLI is MIT licensed, so running the CLI, onboarding, rule writing, and running the underlying ast-grep & Vale checks are all local. You can give it a try with:

npx @taskless/cli

and then asking your agent to "onboard with Taskless".

Under the hood, the CLI works with your agent to read your PR review comments, fixup commits, and agent files. It takes things that keep recurring and turns them into the simplest code-level enforcement that can prevent the issue going forward. By choosing code over an LLM for the runtime, there's no model once code is generated. The checks can then be committed to your codebase and enforced. I'm particularly proud of how determinism is mixed into the onboarding flow. Any time the CLI can give the agent information without letting the agent wandering the codebase, the CLI does. It results in a more consistent experience with far fewer errors. Anonymous telemetry can be disabled outright by setting DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or TASKLESS_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 in your environment (it collects CLI version, OS, the repo's org/owner, and a bit about the repository it's running in).

When the agent's done, it creates a report you can share around to show everyone there's a better way to control the output of agentic coding tools. I thought I'd include a few here from some of my favorite repos.

- Effect: https://tskl.es/gh/Effect-TS/effect/20261104/1g4gRoMmoADlysg... I specifically liked Effect because effect-bot is in the PRs fixing bugs and writing docs for the team, and they already use oxlint plugins and a TypeScript language service plugin.

- Sentry: https://tskl.es/gh/getsentry/sentry/20261016/1ZyMPva1BzaHaa5... Sentry's all open source, and David Cramer's tweeted a lot about determinism, especially now that the team is using Junior to ship code via Slack chat.

- n8n: https://tskl.es/gh/n8n-io/n8n/20261026/1C3I3yVjFyfxNFEpl4qFA... n8n has more AI driven code than the other two repos and is a good example of how bad it can get when the determinism isn't in place. Since agents tend to copy what they see from related files, problems propagate quickly.

I'd love to hear what you're doing today to keep agents behaving, or if you do kick the tires, I'd love the honest feedback.

title.value: Show HN: Taskless, turn AGENTS.md and PR comments into runnable checks

story_text.value:
I'm gonna open this with the disclaimer that this is purely a financial and risk comparison post. No one is complaining that we are poorly compensated. It is good to discuss compensation so we can make informed and educated decisions when deciding how to commit the next few years of our lives.

A close friend of mine joined an AI startup (being intentionally vague) around 1.5 years ago and despite the company doing extremely well on valuation, I'm surprised at how he's not really better off than just working at a large tech company.

Concrete numbers for the startup: -200k salary -Equity grant over 4 years is 500k -The company's valuation has since went from single billions to tens of billions, leaving him with a 10x multiplier when looking only at valuation. After you account for dilution, it's closer to 6x. -Liquidity event annually allows you to sell 10% of your vested shares

Big tech at a similar years of experience is around 400-500k total comp, and the RSU component is generally liquid.

For example sake and ease of calculation, if you assume that my friend's entire equity was vested, and he was able to sell 10% of it, it would amount to approximately $300k/liquidity event, which brings him to around 500k a year as well (200k + 300k). In reality, he's really only able to access $300k/4 since that's all he has vested and that brings him closer to $75k for this liquidity event. There are a lot of variables I'm leaving out obviously such as potential future value, IPO, etc., but the thing that is surprising to me overall is that this is a close to best case outcome, yet the employee doesn't really end up any better off than big tech due to lack of liquidity and dilution. I mean I get it, impact, interesting work, etc. -- the qualitative measures -- aren't really accounted for, but I'm not looking to make a wholistic comparison.

This brings me to the question: Is the risk in a startup ever justified for a lower level employee (engineer, Product Manager, Program Manager, etc.)?

title.value: Ask HN: Are startups today worth it even in a best case scenario?

story_text.value:
When reading of third-party validations of AI's RH proof [0] that:

> While still possible, the proof exploiting a bug is vanishingly small now.

it makes me think we're realising in real-time that we're living through the most important time in human history. Moreso than during the invention of computers, the internet, or the wheel.

Problem: many people worked on RH, and some would have stored their attempts at proofs in places like GitHub or google docs - places that may have been ended up in training datasets.

Therefore, is it possible that Claude knew some significant parts of the proof (potentially even all of it but scattered across multiple private sources) and it merely assembled the parts into a single proof, as opposed to having thought of the proof for itself? [1]

(The distinction matters because assembling parts of existing proofs seems different to authoring a proof by oneself.)

[0] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50590943

[1] I recall AI did something similar with an early Ergos problem (although it used public works), where it found connections and technically solved some unsolved problem, but Terence Tao came out a few days later saying it connected dots but didn't really think of anything truely novel.

title.value: Ask HN: Could AI's RH proof have used human work found in its training data?

story_text.value:
RayClay aims to be the most developer-friendly framework for creating native desktop and mobile applications. It handles all the DIY aspects of C for you while retaining all the performance benefits of using a low-level programming language.

MY MOTIVATION

At the start of the year I decided I wanted to develop my own app with the goal of releasing it on mobile, desktop, and web.

Probably like most developers, I wanted to build a closed-source app and distribute it to whomever I wanted. And I didn't want to have to pay any sort of fee or owe any conditions to the development tools I used. It turns out, this set of criteria really limited what framework I could choose.

Distributing it to whomever I wanted meant that the app had to be properly cross-platform. This cut out options like React Native (no official Linux) and Electron (no iOS or Android). And, while Tauri has yeses for all platforms, I decided that its dependence on platform-native webviews would probably mean excessive ongoing maintenance which I would prefer not to have to deal with. These frameworks were all very bloated anyways so it didn't feel like a big loss tbh.

So I was left with choosing between Qt and Flutter, but Qt has this finicky dual licensing model and Flutter still felt a bit too bloated.

Ultimately, I realised that I was looking for a framework that didn't exist: lightweight like Qt but also convenient and fully open-source like Flutter. I wanted the performance of a lower-level framework with the convenience of less-performant frameworks. Is that really so much to ask for :/

This led me to develop RayClay. It's already 6 months old but now I feel it is really ready for the world to check it out since I've released v1.0 (which I deliberately held back releasing until I though it was ready).

This description is adapted from my blog post here https://www.impizulu.com/blog/why-i-built-rayclay where I give a little more detail.

title.value: Show HN: RayClay – an open source C app framework for desktop, mobile, and web

story_text.value:
I asked rela (the assistant inside my open source crm relaticle) once for a task and a note (in a test workspace). It shows me a plan, one line per change, one approve button. There was no task or note until I clicked approve.

Relaticle (my open source CRM) has an MCP server for AI agents right in the core app. Claude and ChatGPT connect to it, and over the MCP protocol, they don't need a plan, they don't need an approve button, the writes just land right away. Not sure yet if those writes should wait for approval too.

I started writing this in August 2024. It's written in Laravel + PostgreSQL. I'm releasing it under the AGPL-3.0 license. If you want to try it out you can run it using the compose file in the README. I'm very interested in hearing from people who let an agent write to a real system and what they have to say about it.

story_text.value:
I’ve been a listener to the Last Week in AI podcast for years, and come to trust and respect Jeremie and Andrey’s judgment and takes. Jeremie started a new newsletter at AIEndGame.com, and the most recent post is a long prepper article based on his belief that a large scale AI-related attack is very possible. He is much more knowledgeable than I am, and has far more contacts in the AI space at labs and in government, and I’m inclined to trust his take. And the last 6 months of AI developments (HuggingFace hack, various outages in the last two weeks, AI solving Millenium Prize math problems, etc.) have me a bit nervous. On a similar note, the Dwarkesh podcast had a guest this past week that was adamant that we will have AIs in the next 12 months capable of overthrowing governments— which feels hyperbolic, but still.

All to say: is this doomed stuff overwrought and safe to ignore? Or is following this prepper advice a good idea?

story_text.value:
Hello HN. Cordium is a FOSS, self-hosted, identity-based, general-purpose sandbox platform built on Kubernetes. The main differentiator here is that Cordium automatically assigns an identity to each sandbox to provide "secretless" secure remote/zero-trust access to resources/infrastructure (e.g. APIs, SSH, databases, k8s, etc.) without having to hold credentials and secrets (e.g. API keys and access tokens, SSH private keys/passwords, database passwords, mTLS private keys, etc.) inside the sandbox.

The way it works is that every Cordium sandbox includes an Octelium ZTNA client (see https://github.com/octelium/octelium) which routes requests from the sandbox to the upstream resources through the Octelium Cluster running on the same underlying Kubernetes cluster over WireGuard tunnels. In the Octelium Cluster, each upstream resource is protected by a corresponding identity-aware proxy that actually holds the upstream credential that injects the credential on-the-fly to the upstream if the downstream (i.e. the Cordium sandbox) is authorized by an Octelium policy.

In short, Cordium is basically a sandbox platform with a dual nature: it doesn't just provide isolated execution runtimes but it also provides and identity and access infrastructure to provide secure secretless remote access, identity management, L7-aware access control and visibility for every request originating from within the sandbox. You can use it for various use cases from a personal self-hosted GitHub Codespaces alternative for remote development as well as a scalable sandbox platform for AI agents to access infrastructure without handling them your credentials at scale. You can also use it as an infrastructure layer to build more complex applications such as agent meshes.

The main features include declarative management, Templates and prebuilds, persistent, ephemeral and forkable storage via Kubernetes volume snapshots, lifecycle tasks, controls such as linux caps, read-only filesystem and egress control, access and management over web portal/SSH/CLI as well as SDKs in Go/Rust/Python/Typescript. You can learn more about Cordium, its features in detail and how it works, please visit the docs at https://octelium.com/docs/cordium/latest/overview/intro

You can also try a live demo for the Cordium web portal at https://demo.octelium.com/cordium and a CLI playground at https://demo.octelium.com/cli

story_text.value:
I made Admiral. It is a tool to check that Google and Meta ads are working properly. This is its free website check: you don't need an account and no changes will happen on your site. It will ask for a website URL and it will tell you 6 things about it. Each of the 6 is one sentence. If it is "Good" then no change is needed. If it is "Worth fixing" then it says what is wrong.

1. Where you are in search. Admiral will read your pages and tell you, for the searches someone might type in Google to find you, whether you are in the first page on Google. If Admiral cannot work out which words someone might type, it will say that instead of guessing.

2. Whether AI assistants can read your home page. All websites can write a "robots.txt" file that controls what automated search engines and AI assistants are allowed to read. Admiral will read your file to show you which AI assistants are not allowed to read your home page. It cannot ask them any questions so it does not know what they will say about you.

3. Whether your home page will say what your business is. A website can have a hidden message, called "structured data", that tells a web search engine "This page is about a dental clinic in Leeds". Admiral will check whether your home page has this hidden tag for what kind of business you are and what the location is.

4. How fast is your home page on a phone? Google publishes how long each web page took to show during a real visit on Chrome, for websites with enough visitors (the Chrome UX Report). If your site is in there Admiral will use these numbers, if it isn't then it will time its own visit. Also checks if the phone number can be tapped to call.

5. On the main page (homepage), where is the main button? Is the "book now" or "buy" button on the first screen (a screenshot of the homepage)?

6. Is anything checking how much you earn from the advert? It searches for a Google tag or a Meta pixel (these are small pieces of code that ad platforms use to know whether a visit to your website was an enquiry or a sale)

Things you should know about this:

Uses a Google search in your home country. If it's in the US, India, UK, Canada, Australia, Singapore or the UAE that's fine. If it's in any other country, or where this is not possible, a different search engine will be used and it will let you know that this is what another country may see. Only reads your homepage and up to 7 other pages (links off your homepage) and not the whole website. Only reports with sentences instead of a score out of 100. Admiral is paid software, this is free and Admiral is not required. Very interested to hear about the first "what a customer would type" search that gets it wrong on your site.

title.value: Show HN: A free website check that starts from what your buyers search
